strengths: Addresses important and timely research question about the viability of subspace-based safety defenses, with direct relevance to recent alignment work
Rigorous experimental design with four complementary investigations (behavioral expressiveness, selective filtering, geometric overlap, activation patterns) providing strong triangulation
Comprehensive evaluation across 5 different LLMs with proper control baselines (Random-K, Random), both weight and activation space analysis, and multiple evaluation metrics
Remarkably consistent findings across models and experimental settings, suggesting fundamental limitations rather than model-specific artifacts
Clear, well-structured presentation with effective visualizations and logical progression; high reproducibility with promised code release
Technically sound methodology using well-established techniques (SVD, MSO); mathematical notation is clear and precise
weaknesses: Fundamental restriction to linear subspace analysis limits scope of conclusions—safety may exist in non-linear combinations not captured by this framework

Limited model coverage (only open-weight Llama/Qwen models; no GPT-4, Claude) and task diversity (primarily math domain with one safety dataset), raising generalization concerns across architectures and domains
Harmfulness evaluation relies solely on GPT-4o-mini scoring without human validation; limited to 500 AdvBench prompts and single token positions in activation analysis
Lacks statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, significance testing, or multiple runs per model; claims about 'fundamental limitations' would benefit from formal hypothesis testing
Insufficient justification for design choices (SVD fraction ρ, MSO energy threshold η); no sensitivity analysis demonstrating robustness
Limited constructive guidance—paper identifies the problem but offers minimal solutions or discussion of non-linear/hybrid defense approaches that might succeed
Shallow mechanistic understanding of why safety and harmful subspaces overlap; activation analysis doesn't explore position-dependent patterns or attention mechanisms
Key experimental choices lack ablation: contamination ratio (20%) unjustified, sensitivity to hyperparameters unexplored, evaluation limited to math/safety tasks

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study across 5 models with well-designed experiments (weight space, activation space, multiple projections, robustness checks) that rigorously tests the 'linear safety subspace' hypothesis
Important research contribution: challenges assumptions underlying recent defense methods (SafeLoRA, SaLoRA) by demonstrating safety is not linearly separable from general learning
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, clear experimental protocols, promised code release, extensive supplementary materials with per-layer and model-specific analyses
Rigorous methodology with theoretically motivated MSO metric (with analytical random baseline), energy-kept ratio quantification, and proper control experiments (random-K, fully random subspaces)
Consistent findings across multiple experiments, model sizes, and safety training methods (RLHF and DPO), strengthening internal validity of negative results
weaknesses: Limited model scope: only open-weight models up to 7B parameters tested; no evaluation on closed-source LLMs (GPT-4, Claude) or larger models where linearity assumptions may differ

Restriction to linear subspaces only: safety could be encoded through non-linear manifolds, attention mechanisms, or sparse features; limited justification for why non-linear approaches shouldn't be pursued
Narrow evaluation: harmfulness assessed via single evaluator (GPT-4o-mini) with potential prompt sensitivity; utility limited to GSM8K (math only) without diverse downstream task evaluation
Missing direct validation of practical implications: no empirical testing of existing subspace-based defenses (SafeLoRA, SaLoRA, etc.) to confirm they fail as paper predicts

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters (k values, energy thresholds); single runs per model limit robustness claims
Limited mechanistic insight: paper is descriptive (what happens) rather than explanatory (why); does not adequately explain why useful-harmful overlap exceeds alignment-harmful overlap

Constrained experimental design for contamination: single 20% harmful ratio tested; synthetic BeaverTails data may not reflect realistic adversarial fine-tuning scenarios; unclear how findings generalize
Activation space analysis incomplete: only examines last token; missing analysis of early tokens, attention patterns, or layer-specific structures that might show more distinct safety encoding

strengths: Addresses important research question with clear practical relevance: challenges assumptions underlying SafeLoRA, SaLoRA, and similar subspace-based defenses

Comprehensive experimental design with four complementary experiments probing different aspects (weight space projections, contaminated fine-tuning, subspace overlap analysis, activation space analysis)
Rigorous methodology with strong controls (Random-K, Random baselines) and multiple models (5 open-source LLMs from Llama/Qwen families)
Key finding that MSO(Useful, Harmful) > MSO(Harmful, Alignment) provides compelling evidence against safety-specific subspaces—safety isn't uniquely shared between harmful and alignment updates
Extensive validation including per-layer analysis, DPO-based alignment, robustness checks (MMLU, XSTest), and multiple activation space analyses
Clear practical implications: removing alignment-adjacent directions degrades both safety and utility equally, establishing fundamental limitations of projection-based defenses
Excellent reproducibility: code promised publicly available, detailed hyperparameters, extensive appendices (34 pages), clear dataset and experimental specifications
weaknesses: Core finding—safety-learning entanglement—is somewhat intuitive; while comprehensive demonstration is valuable, individual findings are incremental rather than conceptually novel

Restricted to linear subspaces with limited exploration of whether non-linear manifolds or richer representations could capture safety differently; mechanistic understanding of why entanglement occurs is minimal
Limited constructive guidance on alternative defense approaches; paper excels at showing what doesn't work but offers little direction on what might work
Activation space analysis could be deeper: only examines last-generated-token activations; early tokens analyzed briefly in appendix; MSO metric may not optimally capture safety representation

Narrow utility evaluation (MetaMathQA focuses only on math); synthetic harmful data (BeaverTails) may not generalize to real adversarial fine-tuning; GPT-4o-mini scoring introduces evaluator artifacts

Incomplete mechanistic analysis of surprising results: why does Top-K amplify both utility and harmfulness equally? Why is MSO(Useful, Harmful) > MSO(Harmful, Alignment)? These deserve deeper investigation
Key distinctions (e.g., from activation steering literature) relegated to appendices; dense presentation makes some important insights less prominent
Scope limited to open-weight models with single fine-tuning regime; unclear if findings hold across different model scales, training protocols, or closed-source settings
